clue.text: Book, slim part of Bible, poetry without rhyme

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for book
lank means thin and lean
the Bible is divided into chapters and verses

explanation.surface: Someone lists items in a library: a book, a thin section of scripture, some unrhymed poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it read like a list of three items, but the first two run together as the wordplay and the third is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Blank verse is the name for metrical lines, usually iambic pentameter, that do not rhyme, as in Shakespeare and Milton.

clue.text: Auntie looking up and down

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word that looks the same read upwards and downwards is one that runs identically in both directions

parts.note: Auntie is an affectionate British nickname for the BBC, which has another four-letter pet name

explanation.surface: An elderly aunt glancing upward and then downward, perhaps eyeing someone over her spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie (or Auntie Beeb) is a nickname for the BBC, Britain's public broadcaster; BEEB is another, and it reads the same from top or bottom of the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British nicknames for the same national broadcasting corporation, so one stands in for the other.

clue.text: In despair, looking up, seeing part of church

indicators.note: in a down entry, looking up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite of the usual direction
the letters sit inside the following word, so the answer is tucked within it

parts.note: the four central letters of this word

explanation.surface: A despairing person raises their eyes and notices some feature of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: dESPAir holds ESPA, which read upwards gives APSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess, usually vaulted, at the east end of a church beyond the altar.

clue.text: Imminent White House inhabitant treated shark malaria

indicators.note: something treated has been processed or worked on, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A future resident of the White House has been treated for an unlikely tropical disease caught from a shark.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared after the 2020 US election, when Kamala Harris was Vice-President-elect and about to move into the administration.
explanation.definitionFit: At the time she was soon to take office as Vice President, working in the White House, so her arrival there was imminent.

clue.text: Theologian enthralled by opera's musicality

indicators.note: to be enthralled is to be held captive, so the answer is held within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the apostrophe and the word break

explanation.surface: A scholar of religion is captivated by how musical an opera is.
explanation.walkthrough: opERA'S MUSicality holds the name; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch Renaissance humanist scholar who wrote on Christian doctrine and edited the Greek New Testament.

clue.text: Primarily, something offered to herald ending (rude expression!)

definitions.text: Primarily, something offered to herald ending (rude expression!)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives only its opening letter

parts.words: something offered to herald ending (rude expression
parts.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A remark about something said to close an argument, with a note that it is impolite.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word after the comma contributes its initial, including the two in brackets; the whole clue also describes the answer, a cheeky retort that ends a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: This childish, defiant retort is tossed out to close an argument, signalling that the speaker will hear no further objection.

clue.text: Man perhaps somewhat misleading

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following word is used

parts.note: letters two to five of this word

explanation.surface: A comment that a certain man is a little deceptive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person but is the Isle of Man, the island between Britain and Ireland; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is one example of an island, so the general word is defined by a specific instance.

clue.text: Amazing seeing the Queen in second act of vandalism

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: tagging is spraying graffiti signatures on walls
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished to catch the Queen in the middle of defacing property.
explanation.walkthrough: Tagging is spraying graffiti signatures, a British and American term for this kind of vandalism; the royal cipher sits just before its final three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something staggering is so astonishing that it makes you reel, which is close in sense to amazing.

clue.text: In disguise, he'd creep in sneakily

indicators.note: doing something sneakily means doing it underhandedly and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A spy in disguise announces he would slip in unnoticed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a person in costume; the definition is about a message, hidden by being put into code.
explanation.definitionFit: A text that has been encoded into cipher has its true content concealed, as if wearing a disguise.

clue.text: Where you can bet sailors will give you a purgative

parts.note: Epsom Downs is an English racecourse, home of the Derby
old salts are experienced sailors

explanation.surface: A warning that at a betting venue the sailors will dose you with a laxative.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is a town in Surrey, England, whose racecourse stages the Derby; a salt is crossword shorthand for a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom salts, magnesium sulphate crystals, have long been taken dissolved in water as a laxative remedy.

clue.text: Tense? Regularly take garlic powder

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Feeling nervous? A habit of taking garlic powder is recommended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garlic powder' reads as one thing in the surface, but the definition is just the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Talc is a soft mineral ground into a fine white dusting product used on skin.

clue.text: Struggle in France to order foie gras pies

indicators.note: putting things to order means arranging them, so these letters are set out afresh

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in France has trouble ordering pies made with foie gras, the French delicacy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To order' looks like a restaurant request, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prussian army besieged Paris in 1870-71 during the Franco-Prussian War, a prolonged military conflict on French soil.

clue.text: Leg at start of exercise being given circular motion and elevation?

definitions.text: Leg at start of exercise being given circular motion and elevation?

parts.note: a leg is a limb

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
a ring is a circle
up describes being raised

explanation.surface: At the beginning of a workout, a leg is swung round in circles and raised.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a warm-up routine, and the same words also build the answer piece by piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Limbering up means doing loosening stretches and movements before physical activity, like rotating and raising a leg.

clue.text: Jumped-up master, having absorbed a smattering of learning, extremely 'clever Dick'!

indicators.note: to absorb is to take something in, so one piece goes inside another
jumped-up suggests being thrown up into the air and landing jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: a smattering is a tiny amount, so only one letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word

indicators.note: the extremes of a phrase are its two ends, so the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A self-important teacher who has picked up only a little knowledge is a real know-all.
explanation.walkthrough: SMARTE, from MASTER, takes A and L inside to make SMARTALE, and the ends of 'clever Dick' finish it, so the definition doubles as a source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British terms for an irritating person who shows off how much they think they know.

clue.text: Parenting where 'son comes first' is suffocating

indicators.note: coming first means standing at the front, so this piece is placed before the other

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
mothering is raising and caring for a child

explanation.surface: A style of upbringing that always puts the son first is described as overbearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a pointed comment about doting parents, and 'suffocating' fits both the picture and the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Smothering and suffocating both mean depriving of air, and both are used loosely of overprotective care.

clue.text: Everyman is taking speed in Elvis' home

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: the setter of this puzzle is Everyman, who speaks of themself as me
miles per hour, a unit of speed
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to taking amphetamines while visiting Elvis Presley's house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speed' looks like the drug but is a rate, measured in MPH; the setter's pen-name stands for ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley lived in the Tennessee city, at his Graceland mansion, from 1957 until his death.

clue.text: Translation of 'Danger!' before tip of epée is seen?

definitions.text: Translation of 'Danger!' before tip of epée is seen?

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters take a new shape

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the tip of something is its point or end, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fencer's warning cry, in French, given just before the point of the sword appears.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the call is a warning, a 'translation of Danger', uttered before the blade comes at you.
explanation.definitionFit: This French fencing call tells an opponent to take a guarding stance, effectively warning them of imminent attack.

clue.text: Chemists use these witty comebacks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: glass vessels with long downward-bent necks used for distilling

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests chemists trading clever replies; the two halves are separate meanings of the same plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a distilling flask from the laboratory and a quick, sharp answer made in reply to a remark.

clue.text: Wound up about one that's more fearsome

parts.note: a scar is the mark left by a wound
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, the reverse of normal

parts.note: re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone tense and agitated over a person who is even more frightening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' reads as one phrase meaning tense, but the words split: the wound gives the first piece and 'up' acts on 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarier is the comparative of scary, describing something causing greater fright or alarm.

clue.text: Prime Minister that is 7-10 year-old

parts.note: Gordon Brown was UK Prime Minister 2007-2010
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A head of government is described as a young child of primary-school age.
explanation.walkthrough: Brownies are the junior section of the Girl Guides, the girls' scouting movement, for children aged about seven to ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of this junior branch of the Guide movement is a girl in that age range.

clue.text: His most famous character is never performed in modern theatre

definitions.text: His most famous character is never performed in modern theatre

parts.words: His most famous character is never performed in modern theatre
parts.note: surface reading: a playwright whose best-known role somehow never reaches the stage

parts.words: His most famous character is never performed
parts.note: setter's reading: the title figure of his best-known play never appears, since everyone just waits for him

explanation.walkthrough: In 'Waiting for Godot' the two tramps wait throughout for Godot, who never turns up, so the most famous character is never played by anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Beckett, the Irish dramatist, wrote Waiting for Godot, a landmark of modern absurdist drama.

clue.text: Trophy from a ceramics moulding held aloft

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: moulding shapes material into a new form, as clay is reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
something held aloft is up

explanation.surface: A prize made by a potter is raised high in celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moulding' fits pottery so naturally that it hides its role as the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The America's Cup is the famous silver sailing prize awarded in the international yachting race of that name.

clue.text: Whereby type of light starts to enter animals?

definitions.text: Whereby type of light starts to enter animals?

parts.note: UV is ultraviolet light

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so each gives only its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A question asking by what route light gets into creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue hints at the answer: the uvea includes the iris and pupil, through which light passes into an animal's eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The uvea is the pigmented middle layer of the eye, including the iris, which controls how much light comes in.

clue.text: Topic like 'Bigger Moustaches in EastEnders'

indicators.note: EastEnders is set among Cockneys, who drop their aitches, so the phrase must be said in that accent

parts.note: bigger moustaches are hairier, and a Cockney drops the h

explanation.surface: A subject such as a proposed storyline about bushier facial hair on a TV soap.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap set in Cockney East London; 'hairier' in that accent comes out as ''airier'.
explanation.definitionFit: An area can mean a field or subject of study or discussion, as in an area of expertise.

clue.text: Native Americans seeing bear-like characters every so often

indicators.note: characters are letters, and taking them every so often means at intervals, so alternate ones are kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: Native Americans spot creatures resembling bears from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters here, not figures in a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The Erie were an Iroquoian people who lived along the southern shore of the lake now named after them.

clue.text: Amassed much water and industrial kit

parts.note: piled means heaped up
a river is a large flow of water

explanation.surface: A company has stockpiled lots of water along with heavy machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amassed much water' reads as one phrase, but it splits into a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A pile-driver is a heavy machine on building sites that hammers posts, or piles, into the ground.

clue.text: Empty kettle and glass vessels

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its contents, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to drain a kettle and some drinking glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glass vessels' reads as one phrase, but 'glass' is wordplay and the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Kegs are small barrels for holding beer or other liquids, which makes them a kind of container.

clue.text: Wayward youth is behind fiery eruption somewhere in C Europe

indicators.note: being behind means backing or supporting, standing right next to the thing in question

parts.note: a brat is a badly behaved child
taken as written
lava is molten rock thrown out by a volcano

explanation.surface: A delinquent teenager is responsible for a volcanic outburst somewhere in central Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: C is short for Central, so the definition points to a place in central Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Bratislava is the capital city of Slovakia, on the Danube, in the middle of the continent.
